idiom_name: hand-written overload signatures (type-level selection) plus one erased implementation body
implementation_notes: Overload signatures are the closest thing to a tag ladder: the compiler picks the signature that matches the call's static argument types and reports an error when none does, so the selection is visible and checked at compile time. They are erased, though - there is exactly one implementation body, it must handle every case at run time, and the compiler checks the body against the implementation signature only, not against each overload, while type inference for overloaded functions uses the last (most permissive) signature. What replaces the classic structure: an overload signature list plus a discriminated union and a switch inside the single body, or (for type-level selection only) conditional and mapped types, which compute types rather than behaviour. The classic form is justified when the call-site types are closed and the return type differs per case; even then the tag must be carried as a value if the code runs in plain JavaScript.
pitfalls: Overloads are not type-safe: the body is verified against the implementation signature alone, so a missing or wrongly-typed runtime branch compiles cleanly and fails at run time - exactly the guarantee tag dispatching would have given.

A call is resolved to a single overload, so passing a union-typed value requires a union overload and a body that handles every member; otherwise the compiler rejects a call that would work at run time.

The overload ladder exists only for TypeScript consumers: nothing is emitted, so if the module is consumed by plain JavaScript or the value crosses a boundary (JSON, worker, IPC), the tag must travel as a value and the dispatch becomes a runtime check.
Structural type checks (typeof) are unsound at the edges - typeof null === 'object' - so literal discriminant tags on a value are the only reliable tag for the runtime branch.
sources: TypeScript Handbook, More on Functions - Function Overloads (implementation signature is not visible to callers; the body is checked against it), https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/functions.html
TypeScript Handbook, Conditional Types (encoding the choice in types; inference from overloads uses the last signature), https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/conditional-types.html

Michael Rutter, Conditional types and overloading in TypeScript ('function overloads are not type safe ... implementers get no help from the compiler'), https://michaelrutter.dev/conditional-types-and-overloading/
